title: Climbing Stairs
description: Count ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Build from recursion to optimized O(1) space.

data.text: You are climbing a staircase. It takes `n` steps to reach the top. Each time you can either climb 1 or 2 steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top?

**Input:** `n = 3`

**Output:** `3`

**Explanation:** There are three ways to climb:
1. 1 step + 1 step + 1 step
2. 1 step + 2 steps
3. 2 steps + 1 step
At each step, you can take 1 or 2 steps. The total ways to reach step `n` equals ways to reach `n-1` plus ways to reach `n-2`.

data.title: Recursion O(2^n) — Exponential
Why this fails
data.text: Each call branches into two more, creating a binary tree of calls. For n=35, this makes ~27 million calls. The same subproblems are computed repeatedly.
Cache results so each subproblem is solved only once. This turns exponential time into linear.

data.title: Memoization O(n) time and space
What improved here?
data.text: **Time:** Reduced from O(2^n) to O(n) — each value 1..n is computed once. **Space:** O(n) for memo array + O(n) call stack. This is the easiest DP transition: add a cache to recursion.
Build the solution iteratively from the base cases up to `n`. No recursion, no call stack overhead.

data.title: Tabulation O(n) time and space
Tabulation pattern
data.text: `dp[i]` represents the answer for `i` steps. We fill the array from left to right because each state depends only on previous states. This is the standard bottom-up DP pattern.
Notice that `dp[i]` only depends on the last two values. We don't need the full array — just two variables.

data.title: Optimized O(n) time, O(1) space
Best approach
data.text: This is the canonical solution. **Time:** O(n). **Space:** O(1). The pattern of keeping only the last two values applies to many Fibonacci-like DP problems.
